You hear that "the market rose today". Nobody means every company. They mean a stock index, which is a single number standing in for a whole group of shares.

An index picks a list of companies and tracks their share prices together. The FTSE 100 follows the hundred largest firms listed in London. The S&P 500 follows five hundred big American ones. Each day, the prices are combined into one figure, and that figure goes up or down.

Think of a class test average. One pupil's mark tells you little, but the average tells you how the class did overall. An index does the same job for a slice of the economy.

Most indexes weight companies by size. A huge firm moves the number far more than a small one does. So a bad day for a few giants can drag the whole index down, even if most members rose.

The number itself has no meaning on its own. What matters is the change: how it compares with yesterday, or last year. You can also buy funds that simply copy an index, which is why these lists matter to ordinary savers.

In short, a stock index is one number summarising how a chosen group of shares is doing.
